sectionSummaries.summary: This section contains the opening header and date of the maamar.

This section explains that war is called "krav" from the term for closeness, and that the soul's battle with the animal soul during prayer requires the divine soul to clothe itself in the animal soul.

This section explains that the refinement of the animal soul through the divine soul clothing itself is a matter of war, whereas "He redeemed my soul in peace" refers to redemption through the revelation of a supernal light that nullifies the animal soul's desires without war.
It explains that the true meaning of "He redeemed my soul in peace" is specifically through the revelation of the Yechidah.

It questions how after the revelation of the Yechidah, where there is no place for opponents, the Nefesh HaElokis still needs redemption, and explains that this refers to one at a low level who contemplates the Yechidah.

It connects the two types of peace, from above downward and from below upward, to Yaakov's journey and the verse "And all your children shall be taught of Hashem, and great shall be the peace of your children."
This section questions how the maamar can speak of "peace" in both the top-down and bottom-up modes of refinement, when the bottom-up mode is usually associated with struggle.

This section explains that in the top-down refinement the opposing entity is nullified, whereas in the bottom-up refinement the lower entity is refined through its own will and understanding, so its essential opposition remains latent.

This section explains that in the bottom-up refinement the former opponent becomes a lover, a true change in its own existence, whereas in the top-down refinement the lower entity is nullified but not essentially changed.

This section explains that the two types of peace (from above downward and from below upward) must each include the quality of the other, so that the refinement of the animal soul and the world is complete.
This section explains that through contemplation of the Yechidah, which awakens total self-nullification, both modes of refinement include both advantages.
This section connects the above to the Rebbe's father-in-law's explanation that Torah study must be felt as God's Torah, achieved through prayer, which brings peace to scholars and the world.

When Torah study lacks the awareness that it is God's Torah, it can lead to divisiveness rather than peace, as illustrated by a story of a scholar who complained to the Tzemach Tzedek about being trampled upon.
The plural "thoughts" indicates that there are many levels of the thought of selfhood, and even the subtlest thought of a Torah scholar can be a barrier, like a speck of dirt on a garment.

The beginning of avodah is self-nullification, which enables both the upward approach through prayer and the downward approach through Torah study, and the peace of Torah scholars includes the peace of prayer.

Since the purpose of the descent of the sparks is for their refinement, there is no obstacle from the sparks themselves, only from the person doing the refining; the sparks desire to be refined, and through the awakening of the Yechidah this hidden desire becomes revealed.

The peace of refinement through the service of "many were with me" (awakening of the Yechidah) is perfect, encompassing both advantages, because the lower one desires refinement, so the refinement is not contrary to its nature but rather a transformation.

The entire purpose of service is to unite the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah (Sovev and Memaleh), and this is specifically through Yaakov, who possessed the revelation of the Yechidah, enabling the inclusion of both modes of refinement.

This section explains that the Shechinah includes all Jewish souls, and that the unification of the Holy One and His Shechinah also includes the unification of the Holy One and Israel, which will be fully revealed in the future through Mashiach.

sampleTranslations.translation: B"S.
Shabbos Parshas Vayeitzei,
Yud Kislev, Maamar 3,
"He redeemed my soul in peace from the battle that was against me, for many were with me."
And the Baal HaGeulah explains in his maamar beginning with this phrase
(printed in his book Shaarei Teshuvah),
that the reason war is called by the term "krav," from the language of closeness (kiruv)
(even though war is the opposite of closeness),
is,
that the essence of war is that each of the two combatants wants to defeat the other and subdue him so that he will be included within him,
and in order to effect this, that he fights against him so that he will be included within him,
it is specifically through the closeness that he draws near to him,
"krav" from the language of closeness.
And similarly, in the war of the divine soul and the animal soul,
the main war is during the time of prayer
(the time of prayer is the time of battle),
so that in order for the service
(prayer)
of the divine soul to affect the animal soul so that it becomes included in the divine soul
[meaning that the animal soul will also have love of G-d,
"with all your heart, with both your inclinations"],
it is through the divine soul clothing itself in the animal soul,
that the contemplation of the divine soul is in such matters and in such a manner that the animal soul can also grasp them.
However, when prayer is from the aspect of the soul itself,
it does not affect the animal soul,
as explained in the maamar.
Now, the refinement of the animal soul through the divine soul clothing itself in the animal soul,
is a matter of war,
